vsm1.4:87.1:
So in this case it should be understood that seclusion by suppression (suspension) of lust
is indicated by the phrase quite secluded from sense desires,
vsm1.4:87.2: and seclusion by suppression (suspension) of all five hindrances
vsm1.4:87.3:
by the phrase secluded from unprofitable things. But omitting repetitions, that of lust
is indicated by the first and that of the remaining hindrances by the second.
vsm1.4:87.4:
Similarly with the three unprofitable roots, that of greed, which has the five cords of sense
desire (M I 85) as its province, is indicated by the first,
vsm1.4:87.5:
and that of hate and delusion, which have as their respective provinces the various
grounds for annoyance (A IV 408; V 150), etc., by the second.
vsm1.4:87.6:
Or with the states consisting of the floods, etc., that of the flood of sense desires, of the bond of sense
desires, of the canker of sense desires, of sense-desire clinging, of the bodily
tie of covetousness, and of the fetter of greed for sense desires, is indicated by the first,
vsm1.4:87.7: and that of the remaining floods, bonds, cankers, clingings, ties, and fetters, is indicated by the second.
vsm1.4:87.8: Again, that of craving and of what is associated with craving is indicated by the first,
vsm1.4:87.9: and that of ignorance and of what is associated with ignorance is indicated by the second.
vsm1.4:87.10: Furthermore, that of the eight thought-arisings associated with greed (XIV.90) is indicated by the first,
vsm1.4:87.11: and that of the remaining kinds of unprofitable thought-arisings is indicated by the second.
vsm1.4:87.12:
This, in the first place, is the explanation of the meaning of the words “quite
secluded from sense desires, secluded from unprofitable things.”
vsm1.4:88.1: So far the factors abandoned by the jhāna have been shown.
vsm1.4:88.2: And now, in order to show the factors associated with it, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought is said.
vsm1.4:88.3: Herein, applied thinking (vitakkana) is applied thought (vitakka); hitting upon, is what is meant.
vsm1.4:88.4: It has the characteristic of directing the mind on to an object (mounting the mind on its object).
vsm1.4:88.5: Its function is to strike at and thresh—
vsm1.4:88.6: for the meditator is said, in virtue of it, to have the object struck at by applied thought, threshed by applied thought.
vsm1.4:88.7: It is manifested as the leading of the mind onto an object.
vsm1.4:88.8: Sustained thinking (vicaraṇa) is sustained thought (vicāra); continued sustainment (anusañcaraṇa), is what is meant.
vsm1.4:88.9: It has the characteristic of continued pressure on (occupation with) the object.
vsm1.4:88.10: Its function is to keep conascent mental states occupied with that.
vsm1.4:88.11: It is manifested as keeping consciousness anchored on that object.
vsm1.4:89.2: applied thought is the first impact of the mind in the sense that it is both gross and inceptive, like the striking of a bell.
vsm1.4:89.3:
Sustained thought is the act of keeping the mind anchored, in the sense that it
is subtle with the individual essence of continued pressure,
vsm1.4:89.4: like the ringing of the bell.
vsm1.4:89.5: Applied thought intervenes, being the interference of consciousness at the time of first arousing thought,
vsm1.4:89.6: like a bird’s spreading out its wings when about to soar into the air,
vsm1.4:89.7: and like a bee’s diving towards a lotus when it is minded to follow up the scent of it.
vsm1.4:89.8: The behaviour of sustained thought is quiet, being the near non-interference of consciousness,
vsm1.4:89.9: like the bird’s planing with outspread wings after soaring into the air,
vsm1.4:89.10: and like the bee’s buzzing above the lotus after it has dived towards it.
vsm1.4:90.1:
In the commentary to the Book of Twos this is said: “Applied thought occurs as a state of directing the mind onto an object,
like the movement of a large bird taking off into the air by engaging the air with both wings
vsm1.4:90.2: and forcing them downwards. For it causes absorption by being unified.
vsm1.4:90.3:
Sustained thought occurs with the individual essence of continued pressure, like the bird’s movement when it is using
(activating) its wings for the purpose of keeping hold on the air. For it keeps pressing the object”.
vsm1.4:90.4: That fits in with the latter’s occurrence as anchoring.
vsm1.4:90.5: This difference of theirs becomes evident in the first and second jhānas in the fivefold reckoning.
vsm1.4:91.1:
Furthermore, applied thought is like the hand that grips firmly and sustained thought is like the hand that rubs,
when one grips a tarnished metal dish firmly with one hand and rubs it with powder and oil and a woollen pad with the other hand.
vsm1.4:91.2: Likewise, when a potter has spun his wheel with a stroke on the stick and is making a dish,
vsm1.4:91.3: his supporting hand is like applied thought and his hand that moves back and forth is like sustained thought.
vsm1.4:91.4: Likewise, when one is drawing a circle,
vsm1.4:91.5:
the pin that stays fixed down in the centre is like applied thought, which directs onto the object, and the pin
that revolves round it is like sustained thought, which continuously presses.
vsm1.4:92.1: So this jhāna occurs together with this applied thought and this sustained thought
vsm1.4:92.2: and it is called, “accompanied by applied and sustained thought” as a tree is called “accompanied by flowers and fruits.”
vsm1.4:92.4:
the teaching is given in terms of a person in the way beginning, “He is possessed,
fully possessed, of this applied thought and this sustained thought” (Vibh 257).
vsm1.4:92.5: The meaning should be regarded in the same way there too.
vsm1.4:93.1: Born of seclusion: here secludedness (vivitti) is seclusion (viveka); the meaning is, disappearance of hindrances.
vsm1.4:93.2: Or alternatively, it is secluded (vivitta), thus it is seclusion;
vsm1.4:93.3: the meaning is, the collection of states associated with the jhāna is secluded from hindrances.
vsm1.4:93.4: “Born of seclusion” is born of or in that kind of seclusion.
vsm1.4:94.1: Happiness and bliss: it refreshes (pīnayati), thus it is happiness (pīti).
vsm1.4:94.2: It has the characteristic of endearing (sampiyāyanā).
vsm1.4:94.3: Its function is to refresh the body and the mind;
vsm1.4:94.4: or its function is to pervade (thrill with rapture). It is manifested as elation.
vsm1.4:94.5: But it is of five kinds as minor happiness,
vsm1.4:94.9: Herein, minor happiness is only able to raise the hairs on the body.
vsm1.4:94.10: Momentary happiness is like flashes of lightning at different moments.
vsm1.4:94.11: Showering happiness breaks over the body again and again like waves on the sea shore.
vsm1.4:95.1: Uplifting happiness can be powerful enough to levitate the body and make it spring up into the air.
vsm1.4:95.2:
For this was what happened to the Elder Mahā-Tissa, resident at Puṇṇavallika.
He went to the shrine terrace on the evening of the full-moon day.
vsm1.4:95.3: Seeing the moonlight, he faced in the direction of the Great Shrine at Anurādhapura,
vsm1.4:95.4: thinking, “At this very hour the four assemblies are worshipping at the Great Shrine!”
vsm1.4:95.5: By means of objects formerly seen there he aroused uplifting happiness with the Enlightened One as object,
vsm1.4:95.6: and he rose into the air like a painted ball bounced off a plastered floor and alighted on the terrace of the Great Shrine.
vsm1.4:96.1: And this was what happened to the daughter of a clan in the village of Vattakālaka
vsm1.4:96.2:
near the Girikaṇḍaka Monastery when she sprang up into the air owing to strong
uplifting happiness with the Enlightened One as object.
vsm1.4:96.3: As her parents were about to go to the monastery in the evening, it seems, in order to hear the Dhamma,
vsm1.4:96.4:
they told her: “My dear, you are expecting a child; you cannot go out at an unsuitable time.
We shall hear the Dhamma and gain merit for you.” So they went out.
vsm1.4:96.5: And though she wanted to go too, she could not well object to what they said. She stepped out of the house onto a balcony
vsm1.4:96.6: and stood looking at the Ākāsacetiya Shrine at Girikaṇḍaka lit by the moon. She saw the offering of lamps at the shrine,
vsm1.4:96.7: and the four communities as they circumambulated it to the right after making their offerings of flowers and perfumes;
vsm1.4:96.8: and she heard the sound of the massed recital by the Community of Bhikkhus.
vsm1.4:96.9:
Then she thought: “How lucky they are to be able to go to the monastery and wander round
such a shrine terrace and listen to such sweet preaching of Dhamma!”
vsm1.4:96.10: Seeing the shrine as a mound of pearls and arousing uplifting happiness,
vsm1.4:96.11: she sprang up into the air, and before her parents arrived
vsm1.4:96.12: she came down from the air into the shrine terrace, where she paid homage and stood listening to the Dhamma.
vsm1.4:97.1: When her parents arrived, they asked her, “What road did you come by?”
vsm1.4:97.2: She said, “I came through the air, not by the road,”
vsm1.4:97.3: and when they told her, “My dear, those whose cankers are destroyed come through the air. But how did you come?” she replied:
vsm1.4:97.4:
“As I was standing looking at the shrine in the moonlight a strong sense of happiness
arose in me with the Enlightened One as its object.
vsm1.4:97.5:
Then I knew no more whether I was standing or sitting, but only that I was springing
up into the air with the sign that I had grasped, and I came to rest on this shrine terrace.”
vsm1.4:97.6: So uplifting happiness can be powerful enough to levitate the body, make it spring up into the air.
vsm1.4:98.1: But when pervading (rapturous) happiness arises, the whole body is completely pervaded,
vsm1.4:98.2: like a filled bladder, like a rock cavern invaded by a huge inundation.
vsm1.4:99.1: Now, this fivefold happiness, when conceived and matured, perfects the twofold tranquillity,
vsm1.4:99.2: that is, bodily and mental tranquillity.
vsm1.4:99.3: When tranquillity is conceived and matured, it perfects the twofold bliss, that is, bodily and mental bliss.
vsm1.4:99.4: When bliss is conceived and matured, it perfects the threefold concentration,
vsm1.4:99.5: that is, momentary concentration, access concentration, and absorption concentration.
vsm1.4:99.6:
Of these, what is intended in this context by happiness is pervading happiness,
which is the root of absorption and comes by growth into association with absorption.
vsm1.4:100.1: But as to the other word: pleasing (sukhana) is bliss (sukha).
vsm1.4:100.2:
Or alternatively: it thoroughly (suṭṭhu) devours (khādati), consumes (khaṇati),
bodily and mental affliction, thus it is bliss (sukha).
vsm1.4:100.3: It has gratifying as its characteristic.
vsm1.4:100.4: Its function is to intensify associated states. It is manifested as aid.
vsm1.4:100.5: And wherever the two are associated, happiness is the contentedness at getting a desirable object,
vsm1.4:100.6: and bliss is the actual experiencing of it when got.
vsm1.4:100.7: Where there is happiness there is bliss (pleasure);
vsm1.4:100.8: but where there is bliss there is not necessarily happiness.
vsm1.4:100.9: Happiness is included in the formations aggregate;
vsm1.4:100.10: bliss is included in the feeling aggregate.
vsm1.4:100.11: If a man, exhausted in a desert, saw or heard about a pond on the edge of a wood, he would have happiness;
vsm1.4:100.12: if he went into the wood’s shade and used the water, he would have bliss.
vsm1.4:100.13: And it should be understood that this is said because they are obvious on such occasions.
vsm1.4:101.1: Accordingly, (a) this happiness and this bliss are of this jhāna,
vsm1.4:101.2: or in this jhāna; so in this way this jhāna is qualified by the words with happiness and bliss and also born of seclusion.
vsm1.4:101.3: Or alternatively: (b) the words happiness and bliss (pītisukhaṃ) can be taken as “the happiness and the bliss” independently,
vsm1.4:101.5: and so then it can be taken as seclusion-born happiness-and-bliss of this jhāna,
vsm1.4:101.6: or in this jhāna; so in this way it is the happiness and bliss rather than the jhāna that are born of seclusion.
vsm1.4:101.7: For just as the words “born of seclusion” can as at (a) be taken as qualifying the word “jhāna,”
vsm1.4:101.8: so too they can be taken here as at (b) as qualifying the expression “happiness and bliss,”
vsm1.4:101.9:
and then that total expression is predicated of this jhāna. So it is also correct to call
“happiness-and-bliss born-of-seclusion” a single expression.
vsm1.4:101.10: In the Vibhaṅga it is stated in the way beginning, “This bliss accompanied by this happiness” (Vibh 257).
vsm1.4:101.11: The meaning should be regarded in the same way there too.
vsm1.4:102.1: First jhāna: this will be explained below (§119).
vsm1.4:102.2: Enters upon (upasampajja): arrives at; reaches, is what is meant;
vsm1.4:102.3: or else, taking it as “makes enter” (upasampādayitvā), then producing, is what is meant.
vsm1.4:102.4: In the Vibhaṅga this is said:
vsm1.4:102.5:
“‘Enters upon’: the gaining, the regaining, the reaching, the arrival at, the touching,
the realizing of, the entering upon (upasampadā, the first jhāna” (Vibh 257),
vsm1.4:102.6: the meaning of which should be regarded in the same way.
vsm1.4:103.2:
by becoming possessed of jhāna of the kind described above through dwelling in a posture favourable to that jhāna,
he produces a posture, a procedure, a keeping, an enduring, a lasting, a behaviour, a dwelling, of the person.
vsm1.4:103.3: For this is said in the Vibhaṅga:
vsm1.4:103.4: “‘Dwells in’: poses, proceeds, keeps, endures, lasts, behaves, dwells; hence ‘dwells’ is said” (Vibh 252).
vsm1.4:104.1: Now, it was also said above which abandons five factors, possesses five factors (§79; cf. M I 294).
vsm1.4:104.2: Herein, the abandoning of the five factors should be understood as the abandoning of these five hindrances, namely, lust,
vsm1.4:104.6: for no jhāna arises until these have been abandoned,
vsm1.4:104.7: and so they are called the factors of abandoning.
vsm1.4:104.8: For although other unprofitable things too are abandoned at the moment of jhāna,
vsm1.4:104.9: still only these are specifically obstructive to jhāna.
vsm1.4:105.1: The mind affected through lust by greed for varied objective fields
vsm1.4:105.2: does not become concentrated on an object consisting in unity,
vsm1.4:105.3: or being overwhelmed by lust, it does not enter on the way to abandoning the sense-desire element.
vsm1.4:105.4: When pestered by ill will towards an object, it does not occur uninterruptedly.
vsm1.4:105.5: When overcome by stiffness and torpor, it is unwieldy.
vsm1.4:105.6: When seized by agitation and worry, it is unquiet and buzzes about.
vsm1.4:105.7: When stricken by uncertainty, it fails to mount the way to accomplish the attainment of jhāna.
vsm1.4:105.8: So it is these only that are called factors of abandoning because they are specifically obstructive to jhāna.
vsm1.4:106.1: But applied thought directs the mind onto the object; sustained thought keeps it anchored there.
vsm1.4:106.2:
Happiness produced by the success of the effort refreshes the mind whose effort
has succeeded through not being distracted by those hindrances;
vsm1.4:106.3: and bliss intensifies it for the same reason.
vsm1.4:106.4: Then unification aided by this directing onto, this anchoring, this refreshing and this intensifying,
vsm1.4:106.5: evenly and rightly centres (III.3) the mind with its remaining associated states on the object consisting in unity.
vsm1.4:106.6:
Consequently, possession of five factors should be understood as the arising of these five, namely,
applied thought, sustained thought, happiness, bliss and unification of mind.
